newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher on relief trade after PPI.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher on relief trade after PPI.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed higher on Friday as players sighed in relief after the September Producer Price Index (PPI) failed to confirm the market's most pessimistic forecasts, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 15/32 at 98-24/32. Its yield was at 6.85 percent.

Overall PPI rose a mild 0.2 percent in September against a 0.3 percent rise in August. The core rate, which excludes energy and food price fluctuations, was up 0.3 percent last month against a 0.1 percent drop earlier.

"Some people had forecasts calling for a 0.5 percent rise in overall PPI," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank. "Since the forecasts didn't materialize, people jumped back to the market and started buying," he added.
However, some pundits questioned Friday's rally.
They said the buying spree was a result of exaggerated market bearishness before the data rather than the "friendliness" of the economic report itself.
"I think the market may have priced in a more bearish event than what was realized," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Yamaichi International (America) Inc.
Analysts said that a close look at the PPI figures shows some inflationary pressures might still be lurking in the background.

"The core rate of PPI being higher than the overall rate was a surprise. But that was primarily in the auto sector and autos have been pretty good this year," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.

"(But) we have not yet seen the increase in crude oil prices have much of an effect on the overall inflation data. But we're still concerned that it might happen over the next couple of months," Thayer added.
Analysts said that sentiment -- combined with a mixed retail sales report -- prevented a major follow-through buying bout from taking place in late morning and midday trade.
Retail sales rose a surprising 0.7 percent in September.
But analysts said a sharp downward revision to minus 0.2 percent in August from a previously reported 0.2 percent rise offset the bearish headline news.

Still, they said consumer behavior remains the wild card of the economy in the fourth quarter. "I think the issue here is what is the pattern for the fourth quarter ... My sense is that we'll end up with a strong quarter," Strauss said.
Despite Friday's rally, analysts said the yield on the benchmark bond remained within the bounds of a somewhat large range between 6-3/4 and 7-1/4 percent.
"We continued to trade in this trading range ... It looks like that range has worked for the fifth or sixth time this year. That's what this week confirms," Strauss said.

The U.S. Treasury market had an abbreviated session on Friday after the Public Securities Association (PSA) recommended an early close ahead of the U.S. Columbus holiday on October 14. The market will remain closed on Monday.
Trading will resume at normal hours on Tuesday.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down one basis points at 5.01 percent. The six-month bill rate fell five points to 5.10 percent. The year bill rate was down seven points to 5.28 percent.

The two-year note closed up 4/32 at 100-4/32, yielding 5.93 percent. The five-year note traded up 9/32 at 100-10/32 to yield 6.30 percent. The ten-year note closed up 13/32 at 99-19/32, yielding 6.56 percent.
